title: Distinct Subset Products
content: A set $A$ has distinct subset products if every subset yields a unique product. Formally, for all $S, T \subseteq A$ with $S \neq T$, we require $\prod_{a \in S} a \neq \prod_{a \in T} a$. The empty subset contributes the product 1 (the empty product). This is the multiplicative analogue of the classical distinct subset sums problem (Erdős Problem #1).
mathContext: $\text{HasDistinctSubsetProducts}(A) \iff \forall S, T \subseteq A,\; S \neq T \implies \prod_{a \in S} a \neq \prod_{a \in T} a$

title: Injectivity Formulation
content: An equivalent formulation defines distinct subset products via injectivity of the product map $S \mapsto \prod_{a \in S} a$ on the power set of $A$. This is cleaner for Lean's type system since `Function.Injective` is well-supported in Mathlib.

title: The Function g(n)
content: The function $g(n)$ is defined as the maximum cardinality of a subset $A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\}$ satisfying the distinct subset products property. This is defined noncomputably via `Finset.sup` over the power set filtered by the distinct products predicate. A set of size $k$ has $2^k$ subsets, so we need $2^{g(n)}$ distinct products in $\{1, \ldots, n^{g(n)}\}$.

title: Prime Counting Function
content: The prime counting function $\pi(n)$ counts the number of primes $p \leq n$. By the prime number theorem, $\pi(n) \sim n / \ln n$. This function is central to the problem since primes are the building blocks of sets with distinct subset products: by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, any set of distinct primes automatically has distinct subset products.

title: Erdős's 1966 Upper Bound
content: Erdős proved in 1966 that $g(n) \leq \pi(n) + O(\sqrt{n}/\ln n)$, establishing that the prime count dominates. His argument uses the fact that non-prime elements in an optimal set must correspond to prime factorizations that don't create collisions, limiting how many composite numbers can participate. The error term $O(\sqrt{n}/\ln n) \approx O(\pi(\sqrt{n}))$ by the prime number theorem, hinting at the role of prime squares.
mathContext: $g(n) \leq \pi(n) + C \cdot \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\ln n}$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$

title: Erdős's Conjecture
content: Erdős asked whether the natural lower bound from primes and their squares is essentially optimal: $g(n) \leq \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + o(\sqrt{n}/\ln n)$. This would show the second-order term is precisely $\pi(\sqrt{n})$, not just $O(\sqrt{n}/\ln n)$. The conjecture stood open for nearly 60 years, requiring precise control over how composite elements interact in sets with distinct products.

title: Raghavan's Upper Bound (2025)
content: Raghavan's breakthrough establishes $g(n) \leq \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + O(n^{5/12+o(1)})$. The exponent $5/12$ arises from a delicate sieve argument combined with bounds on multiplicative energy. Since $5/12 < 1/2$, this error term $n^{5/12+o(1)}$ is asymptotically smaller than $\sqrt{n}/\ln n$, confirming Erdős's conjecture. The key technique combines additive combinatorics with multiplicative number theory.

title: Raghavan's Lower Bound (2025)
content: The complementary lower bound $g(n) \geq \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + \pi(\sqrt[3]{n})/3 - O(1)$ shows the third-order term comes from cubes of primes. If $p \leq n^{1/3}$, then $p^3 \leq n$ and $p^3$ can be added to the set of primes and prime squares without creating product collisions, since $p^3$ contributes an exponent of 3 in $p$'s factorization—distinguishable from exponents 0, 1, and 2 already present.

title: Conjecture Confirmed
content: Combining the upper and lower bounds pins down the asymptotic: $g(n) = \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + \Theta(\pi(\sqrt[3]{n}))$. Erdős's conjecture follows because $n^{5/12} = o(\sqrt{n}/\ln n)$ (since $5/12 < 1/2$). This resolves a 60-year-old question, showing the primes-plus-prime-squares construction is optimal up to a lower-order term from prime cubes.

title: Primes Have Distinct Products
content: Any set of distinct primes automatically has distinct subset products, as a direct consequence of the fundamental theorem of arithmetic: different subsets of primes produce products with different prime factorizations, hence different values. This gives the baseline $g(n) \geq \pi(n)$.
mathContext: $S, T \subseteq P \text{ (primes)},\; S \neq T \implies \prod_{p \in S} p \neq \prod_{p \in T} p$ by unique factorization

title: Adding Prime Squares
content: Adding $p^2$ for small primes $p \leq \sqrt{n}$ maintains distinct products. Including both $p$ and $p^2$ in the set means the exponent of $p$ in a subset product can be 0, 1, 2, or 3—all distinguishable. The union $P \cup P^2$ where $P$ is primes $\leq n$ and $P^2 = \{p^2 : p \leq \sqrt{n}\}$ has size $\pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n})$.
mathContext: $P = \{p \leq n : p \text{ prime}\},\; P^2 = \{p^2 : p \leq \sqrt{n},\; p \text{ prime}\} \implies |P \cup P^2| = \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n})$

title: Structure of Optimal Sets
content: Raghavan's structural result shows that any optimal set decomposes as $A = P \cup P^2 \cup R$ where $P$ is a set of primes, $P^2$ is a set of prime squares, and $|R| \leq \pi(n^{1/3})/2$. This explains why the function $g(n)$ is dominated by primes and prime squares: composites with multiple distinct prime factors are wasteful because they use up multiple primes' 'slots' for a single element.
mathContext: $A = P \cup P^2 \cup R,\; |R| \leq \frac{\pi(n^{1/3})}{2}$, where all $p \in P$ are prime and all $q \in P^2$ satisfy $q = p^2$ for some prime $p$

title: Error Term Comparison
content: The key comparison $n^{5/12} \leq C \cdot \sqrt{n}/\ln n$ (for large $n$) bridges Erdős's error term and Raghavan's. This is the one theorem Aristotle successfully proved: by choosing $C = n^{5/12} \ln n / \sqrt{n} + 1$ and using the fact that $n^{5/12}/n^{1/2} = n^{-1/12} \to 0$, the bound follows.

title: Multiplicative Sidon Set
content: A multiplicative Sidon set requires that the only way $ab = cd$ with $a, b, c, d \in A$ is if $\{a, b\} = \{c, d\}$. This is strictly stronger than distinct subset products: a Sidon set forbids pairwise product collisions, while distinct products forbids all subset product collisions. The classical (additive) Sidon sets $B_2$ require $a + b = c + d \implies \{a,b\} = \{c,d\}$.

title: Sidon Implies Distinct Products
content: If $A$ is a multiplicative Sidon set then it has distinct subset products, but the converse fails. The implication holds because distinct products is a global condition on all subsets, while Sidon is a pairwise condition. The converse fails: $\{2, 3, 4\}$ has distinct subset products (products are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24) but $2 \cdot 4 = 4 \cdot 2$ gives a trivial Sidon violation from repeated elements.

title: Example: {2, 3, 5} Has Distinct Products
content: The set $\{2, 3, 5\}$ illustrates the primes-only construction. Its $2^3 = 8$ subset products are $1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30$—all distinct by unique factorization. More generally, any set of $k$ distinct primes yields $2^k$ distinct products.

title: Counterexample: {2, 3, 6} Fails
content: The set $\{2, 3, 6\}$ fails the distinct products property because $\{6\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$ both give product 6. This illustrates why composites are dangerous: $6 = 2 \cdot 3$ means including 6 alongside its prime factors creates an unavoidable collision. Optimal sets avoid such redundancy.

title: Small Values of g(n)
content: Computing small values: $g(2) = 1$ (only $\{2\}$), $g(3) = 2$ ($\{2,3\}$), $g(5) = 3$ ($\{2,3,5\}$), $g(10) \geq 5$ ($\{2,3,5,7,4\}$ or $\{2,3,4,5,7\}$—the set of primes $\leq 10$ is $\{2,3,5,7\}$ with 4 elements, and adding $4 = 2^2$ gives a fifth). These match the pattern $g(n) \approx \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n})$ even for small values.
